learn: Geographers use many kinds of maps.
A political map shows borders, countries, states and cities. A physical map shows landforms and water.
A road map shows highways, and a thematic map shows one topic, like population or weather.
check: Which map shows borders and cities?
A map showing only rainfall is a...
lessons.try: Find a political map and a physical map of the United States.

learn: Lines of latitude run east and west around Earth. They measure distance north or south of the equator.
Lines of longitude run north and south from pole to pole. They measure distance east or west of the prime meridian.
Together they form a grid that can locate any place on Earth.
lessons.try: On a globe, find the equator and the prime meridian.

learn: The equator divides Earth into the Northern and Southern Hemispheres.
The prime meridian divides it into the Eastern and Western Hemispheres. The United States is in the Northern and Western Hemispheres.
A map scale lets you calculate real distances.
check: The United States is in the...
A map scale helps you find...
lessons.try: Use a map scale to find the distance between two cities.

learn: Natural resources are things from nature that people use: water, soil, trees, minerals and fuels.
Renewable resources, like trees and sunlight, can be replaced. Nonrenewable resources, like oil and coal, take millions of years to form.
Communities often grow near useful resources.
lessons.try: List five natural resources you used today.

learn: Many cities grew beside rivers, lakes and coasts.
Water provides drinking water, food, farming and transport.
New Orleans grew at the mouth of the Mississippi River, and Chicago grew on Lake Michigan.
check: Why did cities grow near water?
lessons.try: Find three big cities on a map that are next to water.

learn: People adapt to their environment and also change it.
People in cold places build insulated homes. People in dry places use irrigation to water crops.
Building roads, dams and cities changes the land.
lessons.try: Describe how people in your area adapt to the weather.

learn: Native Americans lived in North America for thousands of years before Europeans arrived.
There were, and still are, hundreds of nations, each with its own language, government and traditions.
Many nations, like the Cherokee, Navajo (Diné) and Lakota, are thriving communities today.
check: How long have Native Americans lived in North America?
lessons.try: Find out which Native nations lived or live in your area.

learn: Native peoples used the resources around them.
The Haudenosaunee in the Northeast grew corn, beans and squash, called the Three Sisters.
Plains nations hunted bison and used nearly every part, while Pacific Northwest nations fished for salmon and carved cedar.
lessons.try: Draw the Three Sisters growing together.

learn: Native peoples contributed foods eaten worldwide: corn, potatoes, tomatoes and chocolate.
The Haudenosaunee Confederacy's ideas about uniting nations are often mentioned in discussions of American government.
Native place names are all over the map: Massachusetts, Ohio and Mississippi come from Native words.
check: Which food came from Native peoples of the Americas?
Which state name comes from a Native word?
lessons.try: Find three state names that come from Native languages.

learn: Communities change in population, buildings, transportation and jobs.
A small farm village might grow into a busy city when a railroad arrives.
Historians compare old and new maps and photos to see change.
check: What can cause a village to grow?
lessons.try: Compare an old map of your town with a new one.

learn: New technology changes how people live and work.
Electricity, cars, telephones and the internet changed communities.
Some jobs disappear and new ones appear.
lessons.try: Interview an older relative about technology changes they've seen.

learn: Communities preserve history in museums, historic buildings and monuments.
Local historical societies collect old letters, photos and stories.
Preserving history helps people remember and learn from the past.
check: To remember and learn from the past
lessons.try: Visit a local museum or historic site, in person or online.

learn: An immigrant is a person who moves to a new country to live.
People immigrate to find work, freedom, safety or to join family.
Push factors make people leave, like war. Pull factors draw them in, like jobs.
check: A person who moves to a new country to live
lessons.try: Ask a family member where your ancestors came from.

learn: From 1892 to 1954, over 12 million immigrants entered through Ellis Island in New York.
Angel Island in San Francisco Bay processed many immigrants from Asia between 1910 and 1940.
Immigrants faced long journeys, inspections and sometimes unfair treatment.
check: Angel Island processed many immigrants from...
About how many entered through Ellis Island?
lessons.try: Look at photos of Ellis Island and describe what immigrants experienced.

learn: Immigrants brought foods, languages, music and traditions.
Pizza from Italy, tacos from Mexico and bagels from Eastern Europe are now common American foods.
The country's motto "E pluribus unum" means "Out of many, one".
lessons.try: List five foods from other cultures that your family eats.

learn: Local government runs a city, town or county.
A mayor leads the city, and a city council makes local laws called ordinances.
Local government handles parks, police, libraries, garbage pickup and roads.
lessons.try: Find out who your mayor and council members are.

learn: Each state has three branches: legislative (makes laws), executive (carries out laws, led by the governor) and judicial (courts).
The state legislature meets in the state capitol building.
States run highways, state parks and many education rules.
check: Who leads the state's executive branch?
The branch that makes laws is...
lessons.try: Find your state capitol on a map and the name of your governor.

learn: Governments use taxes to pay for services.
Sales tax is added when you buy things. Property tax is paid on homes and land.
Citizens vote for leaders who decide how tax money is spent.
check: Sales tax is added when you...
Who decides how tax money is spent?
lessons.try: Look at a receipt with a grown-up and find the sales tax.

learn: The Bill of Rights is the first ten amendments to the U.S. Constitution, added in 1791.
The First Amendment protects freedom of speech, religion, the press and peaceful assembly.
These rights protect people from unfair government actions.
check: What is the Bill of Rights?
The First Amendment protects freedom of...
When was the Bill of Rights added?
lessons.try: Name the five freedoms of the First Amendment.

learn: Citizens have responsibilities: obeying laws, paying taxes, serving on juries and voting.
Being informed by reading the news helps people vote wisely.
Respecting the rights of others is a responsibility too.
lessons.try: Make a poster about one civic responsibility.

learn: Citizens can speak at council meetings, write letters to leaders and volunteer.
Children can start projects like recycling drives or park clean-ups.
Petitions collect signatures to ask leaders for change.
check: Collects signatures to ask for change
Can children make a difference locally?
Where can citizens speak to local leaders?
lessons.try: Write a letter to a local leader about something you'd like improved.

learn: Income is money earned from work.
People with more training or rare skills often earn more.
Human capital means the knowledge and skills a person has.
lessons.try: Interview a grown-up about the skills their job needs.

learn: A budget plans how to use income.
Comparing prices helps you get the best value.
Saving for a goal means spending less now to buy something later.
lessons.try: Plan a budget for $20 of pretend allowance: spend, save and share.

learn: Banks keep money safe in accounts.
When you save in a bank, the bank pays you interest, a small extra amount.
When people borrow money, they pay interest to the bank.
check: An extra amount paid on money
lessons.try: If you save $100 and earn $2 interest, how much do you have?

learn: Trade is exchanging goods and services.
Imports are goods brought into a country. Exports are goods sent out.
The United States exports corn and airplanes and imports things like bananas and electronics.
check: Which does the United States export?
lessons.try: Look at labels on five items. Which were imported?

learn: Interdependence means people and countries rely on each other.
A T-shirt might use cotton from one country, be sewn in another and be sold in a third.
If one place has a problem, like a storm, prices can rise elsewhere.
check: A T-shirt might be made in...
A storm in one place can...
lessons.try: Trace the journey of a T-shirt from cotton field to your closet.

learn: Ships, trains, trucks and planes carry goods around the world.
Containers on huge ships carry thousands of products at once.
The internet lets people buy and sell from anywhere.
check: What carries thousands of products at once?
lessons.try: Find a container ship on a map-tracking website with a grown-up.

learn: Culture is the way of life of a group of people: their language, food, clothing, beliefs, art and traditions.
Culture is learned and passed down through families and communities.
Many people share more than one culture.
check: The way of life of a group
Can a person share more than one culture?
lessons.try: Describe three parts of your family's culture.

learn: Lunar New Year is celebrated in China, Korea, Vietnam and elsewhere with family meals and red decorations.
Diwali, the Festival of Lights, is celebrated by Hindus, Sikhs and Jains with lamps and sweets.
Día de los Muertos in Mexico honours loved ones who have died, with altars, flowers and food.
check: Día de los Muertos is from...
Lunar New Year decorations are often...
lessons.try: Choose a celebration from another culture and learn three facts.

learn: Learning about other cultures helps us understand and respect people.
Stereotypes are unfair ideas that everyone in a group is the same.
Asking respectful questions and listening helps us learn.
check: An unfair idea that everyone in a group is the same
How do we learn about other cultures?
lessons.try: Interview a friend about a tradition in their family.
